topic.title: Comment 'LINK' and you work for them
topic.claim: When a creator asks you to comment 'LINK', you're not getting a link; you're doing their marketing for free.
topic.moment: Four thousand comments under a reel, all of them just the word 'link'.

turn.believed: It's an easy way to get the product link.
turn.actually: Each comment tells the app the reel is popular, so it gets shown to more people.

topic.because: Comments push reach, and reach gets the creator paid. The link could just be in the bio.
topic.payoff: Next time, go to the bio. See if the link was there all along.
topic.behaviour: Creators gate links behind comments and auto-DMs; followers comply.
topic.mechanism: Comments drive the algorithm, so creators trade a link for your engagement.
topic.group: Instagram users who shop from reels
topic.send_to: The friend who has commented 'link' on 40 reels this month.

The take's premise is wrong: Premises 1 and 2 both fail as stated, and the conclusion stands on them. Premise 1 says comments are what make the app push a reel to strangers. Instagram's head, Adam Mosseri, named watch time, likes and sends as the top three ranking signals and said sends count most for reaching non-followers. Comments weren't on his list, and he talks about rates per reach, not raw counts. Four thousand identical one-word comments also look like the 'engagement bait' Meta says it demotes. Meta's demotion documentation that I found only covers Facebook, so how Instagram treats these comments isn't confirmed. Premise 2 says reach is what gets the creator paid. For a product reel like this, the creator is usually paid an affiliate commission on purchases (Amazon pays on qualifying purchases, not views or comments), so the comment earns nothing by itself. The 'just put it in the bio' point is only partly true. Instagram allows up to five bio links and shows only the first by default, so a creator posting dozens of products can't list each one there, though a single storefront link could cover them.. How it actually works: Commenting the keyword sets off a tool (typically ManyChat, connected through Meta) that sends you a DM containing a tracked affiliate link. The value to the creator is mainly that DM: it gets you to open a private message thread and puts a trackable link in front of you, which pays them a commission if you buy. Any boost to the reel's reach is a minor side effect and may be cancelled out by demotion of engagement bait. So the comment works less as unpaid labour that buys reach and more as the entry point to a sales pitch aimed at you. Rebuild the post on the correct mechanism.

Says more than the sources: 'Instagram's algorithm counts comments as an engagement signal and treats a reel with many comments as one people are talking about.'. What's true: Comments are a documented ranking signal, but the evidence is weaker for Reels. Instagram says Feed and Stories rank on the likelihood that you will comment, like, reshare and so on. For Reels, its listed predictions are watch-through, likes, 'entertaining or funny' and audio-page visits, not comment volume. A user's own past comments feed the Reels ranking only as an activity signal. Instagram does not say that a reel with many comments is treated as 'one people are talking about'. Mosseri has also said sends/shares matter more than raw like and comment counts. A safer wording: 'comments are one of several engagement signals'. The 2023-05-31 date is the date I recall for the blog post (not shown on the fetched page), so check it..

Says more than the sources: 'Reach is what gets creators paid.'. What's true: Creators are not paid for reach as such. Instagram's payout routes are invite-only performance bonuses (for example the Reels Play Bonus, based on views and engagement), gifts, subscriptions, and brand deals paid by sponsors. The sources I found describe these routes and none says reach itself earns pay. I did not open Instagram's own monetization help pages, so I could not confirm current bonus terms. The claim is too absolute and should be reworded or dropped..

c7.correct: This works through Meta's official Private Replies API, used by third-party tools on professional (Creator or Business) accounts. It is not a native in-app Instagram setting. I did not find a Meta page that promises a response time.

_ledger.text:
[cover] Commenting 'LINK' under a reel is [unpaid work], not shopping
One lowercase word, typed four thousand times, and it isn't for you.
 

[slide 1] Commenting 'LINK' under a reel is unpaid work, not shopping.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] It's late and you're in bed, scrolling. A reel shows a tiny cordless vacuum that fits in a kitchen drawer. The caption says: comment LINK and I'll DM you.
Under it sit four thousand comments, all the same word. You type it too. Lowercase, no full stop.

[slide 3] Seconds later the DM lands. "Hey!! Here's your link 💛".
Fair enough, it does feel like a favour. They saved you a search.
But the app never sees four thousand shoppers. It sees four thousand people who couldn't stop talking about this reel. So it shows the reel to more strangers, who type the same word.

[slide 4] Because reach is what gets a creator paid. Every comment is a push they didn't have to earn with the video itself.
So look at the trade. You get a link that could just as easily sit in their bio. They get your comment, counted by the app, for free.

[slide 5] The next reel will ask for the same word. Open the bio before you type it, and see if the link was there all along.
Then check Your activity, under Comments: 'link', 'link', 'link pls', under reels you can't remember watching.

[end card] Come back to this the next time a caption asks you to comment one word.
The friend who has commented 'link' on 40 reels this month.

[caption] What's the last thing you commented 'link' for, and did you actually end up buying it?

[alt text] A five-slide carousel. Cover: commenting 'LINK' under a reel is unpaid work, not shopping. The slides follow a late-night scroll past a reel of a tiny cordless vacuum with four thousand comments that all say 'link'. You comment too and get a DM with the link seconds later. It feels like a favour, but the app reads all those comments as a reel people can't stop talking about and shows it to more strangers. Reach is what gets creators paid, so you trade your comment for a link that could just be in their bio. The ending suggests opening the bio to see if the link was there all along, then checking your own comment history full of the word 'link'.

462595434fd303c58dd3af9f8c7597780023cbc7.broken_premise: Premises 1 and 2 both fail as stated, and the conclusion stands on them. Premise 1 says comments are what make the app push a reel to strangers. Instagram's head, Adam Mosseri, named watch time, likes and sends as the top three ranking signals and said sends count most for reaching non-followers. Comments weren't on his list, and he talks about rates per reach, not raw counts. Four thousand identical one-word comments also look like the 'engagement bait' Meta says it demotes. Meta's demotion documentation that I found only covers Facebook, so how Instagram treats these comments isn't confirmed. Premise 2 says reach is what gets the creator paid. For a product reel like this, the creator is usually paid an affiliate commission on purchases (Amazon pays on qualifying purchases, not views or comments), so the comment earns nothing by itself. The 'just put it in the bio' point is only partly true. Instagram allows up to five bio links and shows only the first by default, so a creator posting dozens of products can't list each one there, though a single storefront link could cover them.
462595434fd303c58dd3af9f8c7597780023cbc7.actual_mechanism: Commenting the keyword sets off a tool (typically ManyChat, connected through Meta) that sends you a DM containing a tracked affiliate link. The value to the creator is mainly that DM: it gets you to open a private message thread and puts a trackable link in front of you, which pays them a commission if you buy. Any boost to the reel's reach is a minor side effect and may be cancelled out by demotion of engagement bait. So the comment works less as unpaid labour that buys reach and more as the entry point to a sales pitch aimed at you.

cover.headline: Commenting 'LINK' makes you the creator's [free marketing team]
cover.sub: You asked for a link. The app heard applause.

paragraphs: Commenting 'LINK' makes you the creator's free marketing team.
slides.why_swipe: How does one word make you their marketing team?

paragraphs: It's past midnight and your thumb is scrolling on its own. A reel shows a tiny cordless vacuum that fits in a kitchen drawer.
The caption says comment LINK. Four thousand comments sit under it, every one the same word. You add yours. Lowercase, no full stop.
slides.why_swipe: What happens to that reel after you comment?

paragraphs: The link lands in your DMs before you've even closed the app. You forget about it by morning.
Two days later a colleague sends you the same vacuum reel. "Yeh dekha?" They don't follow that creator. The comment count has doubled.
slides.why_swipe: Why did it reach someone who doesn't even follow them?

paragraphs: The app doesn't care what you typed. It counts that you stopped and typed something.
Four thousand people typing the same word looks like a reel everyone is talking about. So the app shows it to more strangers. Your colleague was one of them.
**You didn't ask for a link. You pushed that reel onto your colleague's feed.**
slides.why_swipe: And what does the creator get out of that?

paragraphs: Reach is what pays a creator. Bigger numbers bring brand deals and more sales.

Fair enough, making a good reel is real work, and they should get paid for it. But the link could just sit in the bio. Asking for a comment turns your thumb into their ad budget, and you never see an invoice.
slides.why_swipe: So where was the link the whole time?

paragraphs: Next time that caption asks for one word, tap the creator's name first.
**Often the link is already in the bio, one tap away, sitting there since before the first of those four thousand comments.**

end.save: Come back to this the next time a caption asks you to comment one word.

draft.alt_text: A six-slide carousel. Cover: commenting 'LINK' makes you the creator's free marketing team. Late at night you see a reel of a tiny cordless vacuum with four thousand comments that all say 'link', and you add yours. The link arrives in your DMs and you forget it. Two days later a colleague who doesn't follow the creator sends you the same reel, and the comments have doubled. The app counts that people typed something, so thousands of identical comments make the reel look popular and it gets shown to more strangers. Reach is what pays the creator, and the link could have sat in the bio. The ending: tap the creator's name next time, because the link is often already in the bio, one tap away.
